lines.text: A worker pool signals shutdown with a token, and then one more job gets submitted, right after that signal.
Does that job still get accepted?

tolerated.line: A worker pool signals shutdown with a token, and then one more job gets submitted, right after that signal.

lines.text: No — it's rejected outright, immediately.
A cancelled token isn't a note that gets read eventually. It's a hard stop, checked on the spot.
Run it for real: a handful of jobs land before the signal, and every single submission after it is rejected outright.
Nothing already accepted is touched. The line is drawn at the exact moment the token is cancelled, not before and not after.
Now close a task tracker holding several jobs still in flight, and call wait on it right away.
Does that return as soon as the tracker is closed, or does it actually wait for the jobs themselves?
It waits for every one of them.
Closing a tracker only stops new jobs from being added to it. It says nothing about the jobs already inside.
Run it for real: wait doesn't return until every accepted job has genuinely finished running, measured directly from the close to the moment it comes back.
That's a real wait for real completion, not a signal that completion is merely expected.

lines.text: Wrap that same wait in a real deadline, with one job deliberately running far longer than it.
Does the shutdown hang until that job finishes, or does it stop on time?

tolerated.line: Wrap that same wait in a real deadline, with one job deliberately running far longer than it.

lines.text: It stops on time.
A deadline that doesn't actually end the wait isn't a deadline at all — it's a suggestion.
Run it for real: the wait genuinely stops right at its stated deadline, while the straggler, still unfinished, is simply left behind.
Not waited for a moment longer, and not abandoned a moment early either.
Step back and ask what real-world signal this entire sequence actually exists to answer, in time.
Is it an unhandled crash, or something more deliberate?
A deliberate shutdown request, with a real, limited amount of time to respond.
That's exactly what a termination signal and a grace period are, on a real process, on a real clock.
So here's the full sequence this chapter has now assembled: stop accepting, signal, drain or cancel, close, wait.
Five stages, each one already measured directly, now placed in the order a real shutdown actually runs them.
And every stage of that sequence just used a mechanism this chapter had already proven on its own.
Stop accepting is the token. Drain or cancel is cancel safety. Wait, against a deadline, is the tracker, timed.
So, pulling this topic together: a cancelled token draws a hard line, the instant it's checked, not sometime after.
A tracker's own wait only ever reports real completion, never merely that a stop was requested.
And a stated limit holds exactly where it's set, letting go of whatever hasn't finished by then.
